opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I find fascinating, because I think it's at the heart of why deep learning works at all.

The way I think about it, real data like images or text is not just a cloud of points in a very high-dimensional space. If it were, learning would be hopeless because of the curse of dimensionality. The number of examples you'd need would grow exponentially with the dimension. What saves us is that data has structure, and in particular hierarchical, compositional structure. An image is made of objects, objects are made of parts, parts are made of edges and textures. A sentence is made of clauses, clauses of phrases, phrases of words.

So the key insight is that a good learner shouldn't predict at the level of raw pixels or individual tokens. It should build representations at increasingly abstract levels, where many low-level details become irrelevant. If I want to know whether there's a dog in an image, the precise position of a given edge by a few pixels doesn't matter. The network needs to become invariant to those details while staying sensitive to what matters at the higher level.

In our work we've tried to make this precise with simple generative models of data, for instance what we call random hierarchy models, which are essentially probabilistic context-free grammars. What you find is that deep networks can learn these tasks with a number of samples that is polynomial rather than exponential in the dimension, and the mechanism is quite intuitive. The network discovers that certain low-level features are synonymous, in the sense that they play the same role in the higher-level structure. It can detect this through correlations between those features and the label, or between those features and their context. Once it has grouped synonyms together, it has effectively climbed one level up the hierarchy, and it can repeat the process.

What's interesting is that this tells you something about the sample complexity at each level. Low-level abstractions are cheap to learn because local correlations are strong. Higher-level abstractions require more data because the correlations you need to detect them are weaker and spread over larger scales. So as you increase the training set, the model builds deeper and deeper levels of abstraction, and I think that's part of what we see in scaling laws for language models. With more data, they capture longer-range, more abstract structure.

The same picture is useful for diffusion models. When you add noise to an image and then denoise it, there's a characteristic noise level where the low-level details are lost but the high-level class is still preserved. Beyond some threshold, even the high-level class can change. That's a kind of phase transition, and it reveals the hierarchical organization of the data, and what level of abstraction the model is actually operating at.

So to answer your question directly: I don't think there's one right level of abstraction. The right answer is a hierarchy of levels, and the remarkable thing about deep networks is that they can discover that hierarchy from data. The open questions for me are to understand how much data is required to reach a given level, and whether current architectures are efficient at doing it or whether they still waste a lot of samples relative to what's theoretically possible.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare how many words human brains and machines learn from.

r002.rationale: It directly contrasts predicting raw pixels or tokens with learning increasingly abstract representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, this is really the central question for me, and I think the honest answer is that the machine shouldn't predict at a single level of abstraction. It should predict at all of them, and the interesting structure is in how those levels are organized.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at real data, images, language, physical systems, they are compositional and hierarchical. A sentence is made of phrases, phrases are made of words, words of characters. An image has objects, objects have parts, parts have edges and textures. And crucially, the high-level features are not simply the sum of the low-level ones. There is a many-to-one mapping going up. Many different pixel configurations correspond to the same "cat ear", and many different arrangements of ears and whiskers correspond to "cat". So each level of abstraction throws away information that is irrelevant for the level above it. That invariance is really what abstraction is.

Now, why does this matter for learning? Because the curse of dimensionality tells you that if you try to learn a function of, say, a million pixels directly, you need an astronomical amount of data. No one could ever learn that. But if the task has this hierarchical structure, then you can learn it piece by piece. You first learn which low-level patterns are synonyms, interchangeable with respect to the next level up. Once you have collapsed those, the problem at the next level is effectively lower-dimensional, and you repeat. What we found, with simple generative models of this type, random hierarchy models as we call them, is that the number of training examples needed to learn such a task is polynomial in the dimension rather than exponential. And that the sample complexity is controlled essentially by the number of examples needed to detect that two low-level features map to the same thing. So abstraction is not a philosophical nicety, it is the mechanism by which learning becomes possible at all.

And the second point is that I think deep networks actually learn this way, more or less. If you look inside a trained network, the early layers become invariant to the low-level synonyms, and this invariance propagates upward as training proceeds. So the depth of the network is really tracking the depth of the hierarchy in the data. Which means the right question is maybe not "which level should the machine predict at", but rather "does the architecture and the training have enough room to build the whole ladder of abstractions, from the data, without being told what the levels are". That, I think, is the real game.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare how many words human brains and machines learn from.

r002.rationale: It frames the question as which level a machine should predict at and contrasts low-level features with higher-level abstractions.

astra-6.text:
I think the important question is: what do you need to predict? If you try to predict the world at the level of every pixel, you spend an enormous amount of effort on details that may be irrelevant to what you want to do. If I move a glass across a table, for example, you might want to predict where the glass will end up, without predicting every reflection on its surface.

But then the difficulty is to learn the right variables. You cannot simply say, “We should predict at an abstract level,” because finding that level is itself part of the problem. And if you make the representation too abstract, you can throw away information that matters later.

So I would expect that you need several levels, with some connection between them. You want a description that makes prediction simpler, but that remains grounded in observations. From a physics perspective, this is very familiar: a useful description does not retain every microscopic detail. It retains the variables that allow you to understand the behavior you care about. The challenge for learning is to discover those variables rather than have us specify them.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not mention human brains, language learning, or a comparison in the number of words learned.

r002.rationale: It contrasts predicting every pixel with predicting higher-level variables or abstractions, directly addressing which level machines should predict.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is: predict what? If you try to predict every detail of the sensory input, you may spend most of your resources on things that are essentially irrelevant. Imagine watching a tree moving in the wind. Predicting the precise position of every leaf is extremely difficult, but that may tell you very little about what you should do next.

So you would like to predict at a level of abstraction where the variables are both reasonably predictable and useful. But then you have a circular problem: to learn good representations, you need some notion of what matters; and to know what matters, you need some understanding of the world.

My feeling is that prediction and learning representations have to go together, probably at several timescales. At a short timescale, details can be useful. At a longer timescale, you need more abstract variables. The challenge is to learn those variables without specifying in advance what they should be, while also avoiding representations that make prediction easy simply by throwing away all the information.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare how many words humans and machines learn from.

r002.rationale: It asks what machines should predict and contrasts predicting every sensory detail with learning useful, more abstract variables.
